title: 🕵️‍♂️ Can AI Detectors Really Know Who Wrote It?
ig_caption:
“AI detectors” don’t detect AI… they detect *risk-avoiding writing patterns*.
Here’s what they actually do—and why they miss.

• A detector is basically a classifier with a probability score
• It scans text for statistical fingerprints (entropy, burstiness, repetition)
• It also looks for “tells” of smoothness: predictable phrasing + low surprise
• Under the hood: features → model → AI-probability meter
• If it crosses a threshold, it flags “AI-written”
• But thresholds assume the world is stable (it isn’t)
• Human writing is also pattern-driven—so false positives happen
• Different models, prompts, and editing style change the fingerprints
• Result: detectors catch “plays it safe,” not “machine authorship”

Practical takeaway: If you’re building an evaluation pipeline, don’t treat detector output as ground truth—log it as *one signal* and calibrate on your own domain data.

What should we trust more in high-stakes settings: detector confidence, or provenance (process + audit trails)?

fb_caption:
Most “AI detectors” are not forensic tools—they’re classifiers.

Under the hood, an AI detector typically:
- Tokenizes and computes text statistics (e.g., predictability/entropy, distributional regularities)
- Extracts heuristic or learned features tied to “surface style” (smoothness, low variance, reduced surprisal)
- Feeds those into a model that outputs an AI-likelihood score
- Applies a threshold to produce the binary label (“AI-written”)
- Exposes an “AI-probability meter” that people interpret like evidence

Why they fail
- They optimize for a narrow training distribution: “common AI outputs” vs your real-world text.
- They detect *writing behavior* (“plays it safe”) rather than authorship.
- Editing and rewriting shift statistical fingerprints dramatically, even when the author is human.
- Human writing frequently overlaps with the same statistical signals (templates, coaching, constrained drafts).
- The threshold is a policy decision, not a truth detector: small calibration changes flip outcomes.

The bigger engineering lesson
If you’re designing systems that rely on “AI detection,” treat detector output as:
- A weak signal in a larger risk model, not ground truth
- Something you must calibrate and continuously monitor
- Something you should pair with provenance and process evidence (version history, timestamps, draft lineage, authorship attestations)

Production trade-offs to consider:
- False positives harm legitimate users; false negatives undermine moderation.
- Domain drift (new models, new prompt styles, new editorial conventions) will degrade performance.
- Explainability is limited: a score is not a narrative of who wrote it.

Practical interview tip: When discussing detectors, frame the conversation as evaluation + calibration + threat modeling. Ask how you would measure drift, set thresholds, and combine signals.

Debate question: Should “AI-written” labeling be allowed in high-stakes decisions unless provenance/audit trails are present—or can we rely on probabilistic detectors alone?
